advances: The uniform ternary divergence law of every finite oriented multigraph has its largest fiber at zero. A product of the ranges of independent vertex equations therefore gives a reflected-support lower bound on every edge-deleted subgraph, without grouping distinct columns. The bound applies pointwise to every actual containing cap through the accepted reflection inequality. This establishes a graphical counting bridge, not a universal cubic moment or the locked target.

proof:
We first prove a stronger centered counting statement, solely to make an induction closed under taking pair sums. All matrices in this part are the full incidence matrix \(\widehat A\).

For nonnegative integer capacities \(\mathbf a=(a_e)_{e\in E}\), define the centered edge set \(T(a_e):=\{-a_e/2,-a_e/2+1,\ldots,a_e/2\}\), and let
\(f_{\mathbf a}(\mathbf b):=|\{\mathbf x\in\prod_{e\in E}T(a_e):\widehat A\mathbf x=\mathbf b\}|\).
Suppose that the weighted degree \(\sum_{e\ni v}a_e\) is even at every vertex \(v\). Then every allowed \(\mathbf x\) has integer divergence: write \(\mathbf x=\mathbf n-\mathbf a/2\) with \(\mathbf n\) integer, and note that each entry of \(\widehat A\mathbf a\) is even, since its reduction modulo \(2\) equals the weighted degree. We claim that
\(f_{\mathbf a}(\mathbf b)\le f_{\mathbf a}(\mathbf0)\) for every \(\mathbf b\in\mathbb Z^V\).

First, \(f_{\mathbf a}(\mathbf0)\ge1\). The subgraph formed by the edges with odd \(a_e\) has even degree at every vertex. It can be decomposed into closed trails: follow unused edges until no extension is possible; the endpoint must be the starting vertex, because at any other endpoint the used incident degree is odd whereas the original degree is even, leaving an unused incident edge. Remove the closed trail, preserving even degrees, and repeat. Orient each trail in its traversal direction. Each vertex then has equally many incoming and outgoing odd-capacity edges. On such an edge take \(x_e=1/2\) if the traversal agrees with its fixed orientation and \(x_e=-1/2\) otherwise. On every even-capacity edge take \(x_e=0\). These values belong to their respective \(T(a_e)\) and have divergence zero.

We prove the claim by induction on \(\sum_e a_e\). If that sum is zero, there is only the zero assignment and the claim holds. For the inductive step, negation gives \(f_{\mathbf a}(-\mathbf b)=f_{\mathbf a}(\mathbf b)\). Count ordered pairs \((\mathbf x,\mathbf y)\) with divergences \(\mathbf b\) and \(-\mathbf b\), respectively. Their sum \(\mathbf w:=\mathbf x+\mathbf y\) is an integer circulation satisfying \(|w_e|\le a_e\). Define the finite set
\(W_{\mathbf a}:=\{\mathbf w\in\mathbb Z^E:\widehat A\mathbf w=\mathbf0,\ |w_e|\le a_e\text{ for all }e\}\).

Fix \(\mathbf w\in W_{\mathbf a}\), and put \(a'_e:=a_e-|w_e|\). The coordinatewise correspondence
\[
\mathbf x=\frac{\mathbf w}{2}+\mathbf t,
\qquad
\mathbf y=\frac{\mathbf w}{2}-\mathbf t
\]
is a bijection between the pairs with this sum and the assignments \(\mathbf t\in\prod_e T(a'_e)\) satisfying \(\widehat A\mathbf t=\mathbf b\). To check the edge sets exactly, the conditions \(x_e\in T(a_e)\) and \(w_e-x_e\in T(a_e)\) give an interval with center \(w_e/2\), radius \((a_e-|w_e|)/2\), and step \(1\). Its translated lattice is precisely \(T(a'_e)\), because \(a_e+w_e\equiv a_e-|w_e|\pmod2\). The divergence assertion follows from \(\widehat A\mathbf w=\mathbf0\).

The residual capacities satisfy the required even-degree hypothesis. Indeed, at every vertex, working modulo \(2\),
\[
\sum_{e\ni v}a'_e
\equiv \sum_{e\ni v}a_e-\sum_{e\ni v}|w_e|
\equiv -\sum_{e\ni v}w_e
\equiv -(\widehat A\mathbf w)_v
\equiv0\pmod2.
\]
The unsigned and incidence-signed sums agree modulo \(2\). If \(\mathbf w\ne\mathbf0\), then \(\sum_e a'_e<\sum_e a_e\), so the induction hypothesis applies to \(f_{\mathbf a'}\).

For \(\mathbf w=\mathbf0\), the pairs are exactly \((\mathbf x,-\mathbf x)\), of which there are \(f_{\mathbf a}(\mathbf b)\). Thus the pair count yields the exact identities
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_{\mathbf a}(\mathbf b)^2-f_{\mathbf a}(\mathbf b)
&=\sum_{\substack{\mathbf w\in W_{\mathbf a}\\\mathbf w\ne\mathbf0}}
f_{\mathbf a-|\mathbf w|}(\mathbf b)\\
&\le\sum_{\substack{\mathbf w\in W_{\mathbf a}\\\mathbf w\ne\mathbf0}}
f_{\mathbf a-|\mathbf w|}(\mathbf0)
=f_{\mathbf a}(\mathbf0)^2-f_{\mathbf a}(\mathbf0).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(\mathbf a-|\mathbf w|\) is componentwise subtraction. Since \(f_{\mathbf a}(\mathbf0)\ge1\), the last inequality implies \(f_{\mathbf a}(\mathbf b)\le f_{\mathbf a}(\mathbf0)\): if the first integer count exceeded the second, its value of \(u(u-1)\) would be strictly larger. This completes the induction. No multivariate log-concavity is used.

Set \(a_e=2\) on every edge. Then \(T(a_e)=\{-1,0,1\}\), and all weighted degrees are even. The claim proves central dominance for the full incidence matrix. If \(A\) omits one vertex row per component, a prescribed reduced divergence has a unique full completion: the missing coordinate is minus the sum of the prescribed coordinates in that component. Every full incidence divergence has component sum zero, so its full and reduced fibers coincide under this completion. The completion of zero is zero, proving central dominance for the stated row-reduced matrix as well.

We next justify the row-range bound. The rows indexed by \(J\) are independent. If a linear combination of these rows is zero, extend its vertex coefficients by zero at the omitted vertices. On every edge the two endpoint coefficients must agree. They are therefore constant on each connected component and zero at its omitted vertex, hence all zero. Conversely, the sum of the full rows within each component is zero, giving \(\operatorname{rank}\widehat A=|J|\). Specifying a divergence on \(J\) determines all its other coordinates by the component-sum equations.

For a ternary edge assignment, each divergence coordinate at \(v\in J\) lies in the integer interval \([-\deg_G(v),\deg_G(v)]\). There are at most \(\prod_{v\in J}(2\deg_G(v)+1)\) possible tuples. The \(3^N\) assignments are partitioned into these fibers, each of size at most \(c_G(\mathbf0)\) by the result just proved. This gives the degree-product bound and its ceiling. Replacing every degree by \(\Delta_G\) gives the rank/maximum-degree bound. The proof also covers isolated vertices and the empty graph.

Finally fix \(\mathbf z\in D\) and its zero-coordinate set \(I\). Coordinatewise ternary reflection forces \(x_e=z_e\) whenever \(z_e\ne0\), and imposes no extra coordinate restriction when \(z_e=0\). Since \(A\mathbf z=\mathbf0\) and \(z_e=0\) on \(I\), the fixed coordinates outside \(I\) themselves contribute divergence zero. Thus, after fixing them, \(A\mathbf x=\mathbf0\) is equivalent to \(A_I\mathbf x_I=\mathbf0\), and the reflected vector has the same property. The omitted-row component-sum argument also shows \(A_I\mathbf x_I=\mathbf0\) if and only if \(\widehat A_I\mathbf x_I=\mathbf0\). Restriction to \(I\) is consequently a bijection from \(R_{\mathbf z}\) to the ternary zero-flow fiber of \(G_I\). This proves the displayed description of \(R_{\mathbf z}\) and the exact identity \(k_{\mathbf z}=c_{G_I}(\mathbf0)\).

Apply the row-range bound to \(G_I\) to get \(k_{\mathbf z}\ge3^m/Q_I\). Negation pairs every nonzero zero-flow assignment with a distinct assignment and fixes only the all-zero assignment. Therefore \(k_{\mathbf z}\) is odd, and \((k_{\mathbf z}+1)/2\) is an integer at least \((1+3^m/Q_I)/2\). This proves \(k_{\mathbf z}\ge2L_I-1\). The rank/degree specialization follows as before. For a given component, all choices of omitted vertex have row product equal to the product over its vertices divided by the factor belonging to the omitted vertex. Omitting a maximum-degree vertex therefore minimizes that product.

Accepted fact \(\texttt{ebb695e93a721952}\), applied with exactly the present \(D,p,R_{\mathbf z},k_{\mathbf z},B_{\mathbf z}\), gives, for every closed halfspace \(H\ni\mathbf z\),
\[
|E_{\mathbf z,H}|\ge\frac{k_{\mathbf z}+1}{2},
\qquad
\sum_{\mathbf x\in D\cap H}p_{\mathbf x}
\ge\frac{|E_{\mathbf z,H}|^2p_{\mathbf z}^2}{B_{\mathbf z}}
\ge\frac{L_I^2p_{\mathbf z}^2}{B_{\mathbf z}}.
\]
For completeness, the minimum count is attained by a through-root halfspace whose normal is nonorthogonal to every nonzero difference \(\mathbf x-\mathbf z\) with \(\mathbf x\in R_{\mathbf z}\). Such a normal exists: normals \((1,t,\ldots,t^{N-1})\) violate a given nonzero difference only at the finitely many zeros of its nonzero polynomial in \(t\); avoid the union of those finite sets. Each reflected pair then contributes exactly one point and the root contributes one, giving \((k_{\mathbf z}+1)/2\). This is a count-minimizing cap, not an assertion about which cap minimizes weighted mass. The weighted inequality already holds for every cap, including nongeneric minimizing caps and all their boundary atoms. Minimizing its left side gives the stated bound on \(\tau_p\). When \(I\) is empty there is only the empty zero-flow assignment, yielding all the stated empty-product values.
statement:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite loopless oriented multigraph with \(N=|E|\). Degrees and connected components refer to its underlying undirected multigraph; isolated vertices are components. Let \(\widehat A\) be its full incidence matrix, with entries \(-1\) at an edge's tail and \(+1\) at its head. Let \(A\) be either \(\widehat A\) or the matrix obtained by omitting one vertex row from each connected component. Thus \(\widehat A=A\) in the full-row case. For every integer vector \(\mathbf b\) of the row dimension of \(A\), define \(c_G(\mathbf b):=|\{\mathbf x\in\{-1,0,1\}^{E}:A\mathbf x=\mathbf b\}|\). Then \(c_G(\mathbf b)\le c_G(\mathbf0)\).

Let \(J\subseteq V\) be obtained by omitting one vertex from each connected component, and put \(r=|J|=\operatorname{rank}\widehat A\). These vertex rows are independent, and
\[
c_G(\mathbf0)\ge
\left\lceil\frac{3^N}{\prod_{v\in J}(2\deg_G(v)+1)}\right\rceil
\ge \frac{3^N}{(2\Delta_G+1)^r},
\qquad
\Delta_G:=\max_{v\in V}\deg_G(v).
\]
If \(V=\varnothing\), set \(\Delta_G=0\); empty products are \(1\). The counting statements include \(N=0\).

For the reflection application, assume \(N\ge1\), put \(D:=\{\mathbf x\in\{-1,0,1\}^{E}:A\mathbf x=\mathbf0\}\), and let \(\boldsymbol\ell\in\mathbb R^E\). Use exactly the canonical definitions in accepted fact \(\texttt{ebb695e93a721952}\):
\[
p_{\mathbf x}:=\frac{e^{\boldsymbol\ell\cdot\mathbf x}}{\sum_{\mathbf y\in D}e^{\boldsymbol\ell\cdot\mathbf y}},
\qquad
\tau_p(\mathbf z):=\min_{\substack{H\text{ a closed halfspace in }\mathbb R^E\\\mathbf z\in H}}
\sum_{\mathbf x\in D\cap H}p_{\mathbf x},
\]
and \(R_{\mathbf z}:=\{\mathbf x\in D:2\mathbf z-\mathbf x\in D\}\), \(k_{\mathbf z}:=|R_{\mathbf z}|\), and \(B_{\mathbf z}:=\sum_{\mathbf x\in R_{\mathbf z}}p_{\mathbf x}\). Halfspaces have nonzero normals.

For any \(\mathbf z\in D\), let \(I:=\{e\in E:z_e=0\}\), \(m:=|I|\), and \(G_I:=(V,I)\), with the inherited orientations. Choose \(J_I\) by omitting one vertex from each connected component of \(G_I\), including each isolated vertex, and define
\[
Q_I:=\prod_{v\in J_I}(2\deg_{G_I}(v)+1),
\qquad
L_I:=\left\lceil\frac{1+3^m/Q_I}{2}\right\rceil,
\qquad
r_I:=|J_I|=\operatorname{rank}\widehat A_I.
\]
Here \(\widehat A_I\) is the full incidence matrix restricted to columns in \(I\). The count \(c_{G_I}(\mathbf0)\) may use this full matrix or a row basis for \(G_I\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_{\mathbf z}&=\{\mathbf x\in D:x_e=z_e\text{ for every }e\notin I\},\\
k_{\mathbf z}&=c_{G_I}(\mathbf0)\ge 2L_I-1\ge\frac{3^m}{Q_I}
\ge\frac{3^m}{(2\Delta_{G_I}+1)^{r_I}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(E_{\mathbf z,H}:=R_{\mathbf z}\cap H\), the exact minimum reflected cap count and the pointwise weighted cap bound are
\[
\min_{H\ni\mathbf z}|E_{\mathbf z,H}|=\frac{k_{\mathbf z}+1}{2}\ge L_I,
\qquad
\sum_{\mathbf x\in D\cap H}p_{\mathbf x}\ge
\frac{L_I^2p_{\mathbf z}^2}{B_{\mathbf z}}
\quad\text{for every closed halfspace }H\ni\mathbf z.
\]
Consequently \(\tau_p(\mathbf z)\ge L_I^2p_{\mathbf z}^2/B_{\mathbf z}\). In particular, a halfspace minimizing the actual depth has this same lower bound, without a generic-normal assumption. Omitting a maximum-degree vertex of each component minimizes \(Q_I\) among these row-basis choices. If \(I=\varnothing\), then \(Q_I=L_I=k_{\mathbf z}=1\) and \(r_I=0\).
